fields.Front: Who invented packet switching, and what were the first ARPAnet milestones?
fields.Back:
Leonard Kleinrock (MIT, 1961) used queueing theory to show packet switching suits bursty traffic; Paul Baran (RAND) and Donald Davies (NPL, UK) had the idea independently.
ARPAnet: first packet switch installed at UCLA in 1969 (four nodes by end of 1969); ~15 nodes, the NCP host-to-host protocol and the first email program (Ray Tomlinson) by 1972.

fields.Front: Summarize the internetworking era (1972-1980): who designed TCP/IP, what ALOHAnet and Ethernet contributed, and when TCP/IP replaced NCP.
fields.Back:
Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn (1974) designed the architecture for interconnecting networks ('internetting'); after IP was split out, TCP, UDP and IP were in place by the end of the 1970s.
ALOHAnet (Hawaii, Abramson) gave the first multiple-access protocol for a shared radio medium; Metcalfe and Boggs built on it to create Ethernet (1976).
TCP/IP replaced NCP on ARPAnet on January 1, 1983 (flag day).

fields.Front: What happened to the ARPAnet in 1967, 1969 and 1972? (Kurose §1.7.1)
fields.Back:
1967: Lawrence Roberts (with J. C. R. Licklider, both ex-MIT colleagues of Kleinrock, leading ARPA's computer science program) publishes the overall plan for the ARPAnet.
1969: on Labor Day the first packet switch is installed at UCLA under Kleinrock's supervision; three more follow at SRI, UC Santa Barbara and the University of Utah - four nodes by year end. The first use was a remote login from UCLA to SRI that crashed the SRI host after 'L', 'o', 'g', so the first message was 'Lo'.
1972: about 15 nodes; Robert Kahn gives the first public demonstration; the NCP (network-control protocol) host-to-host protocol is completed; and, because an end-to-end protocol now existed, Ray Tomlinson writes the first e-mail program.

fields.Front: What did ALOHAnet contribute, and how did it lead to Ethernet? (Kurose §1.7.2)
fields.Back:
ALOHAnet (Norman Abramson, Hawaii, 1970) was a packet radio network linking sites across the Hawaiian islands. The ALOHA protocol was the FIRST multiple-access protocol, letting geographically distributed users share a single broadcast medium (one radio frequency).
Metcalfe and Boggs built directly on that work to develop Ethernet in 1976 for wire-based shared broadcast networks. Their motivation was mundane - connecting multiple PCs, printers and shared disks - which laid the foundation for PC LANs before the PC revolution.
Other networks of the era: DARPA packet-satellite and packet-radio, Telenet (BBN), Cyclades (Louis Pouzin, France), Tymnet, IBM's SNA.

fields.Front: What was Minitel, and why does the textbook mention it? (Kurose §1.7.3)
fields.Back:
A French government project of the early 1980s to bring data networking into every home: a public packet-switched network based on the X.25 protocol suite, Minitel servers, and cheap terminals with built-in low-speed modems.
It took off in 1984 when the government gave a free terminal to every household that wanted one, and at its mid-1990s peak offered more than 20,000 services, from home banking to research databases.
The point: the Minitel was in a large proportion of French homes ten years before most Americans had heard of the Internet - consumer data networking was not invented by the Web.

fields.Front: Summarize the new millennium (2000s onward) in the five developments the textbook singles out. (Kurose §1.7.5)
fields.Back:
1) Aggressive broadband residential access - cable, DSL, fibre to the home, 5G fixed wireless, LEO satellites - which is what enabled video (YouTube, TikTok, Netflix, Zoom).
2) Ubiquitous high-speed wireless, enabling location-specific applications (maps, ride-sharing, delivery, dating); the number of wireless devices surpassed wired devices in 2011.
3) Online social networks built on top of the Internet, which through their APIs became platforms for further applications.
4) Content-provider private networks (Google, Microsoft) that connect their data centers and bypass the public Internet by peering directly with lower-tier ISPs.
5) Cloud computing (Amazon EC2, Azure, Alibaba Cloud), which also gives applications implicit access to those private networks.

fields.Text: Packet switching was first published by {{c1::Leonard Kleinrock}} in {{c1::1961}}; the ARPAnet's first packet switch was installed at {{c1::UCLA}} in {{c1::1969}}; the first email program was written by {{c1::Ray Tomlinson}} in 1972.
{{c1::TCP/IP}} replaced {{c1::NCP}} on the ARPAnet on {{c1::January 1, 1983}}; the Web was invented by {{c1::Tim Berners-Lee}} at {{c1::CERN}} in 1989-1991.

1990s: NSFNET allowed commercial use in {{c1::1991}} and was decommissioned in {{c1::1995}}; the Web's four components were {{c1::HTML, HTTP, a Web server, a browser}}; the decade's killer apps were {{c1::email, the Web, instant messaging, P2P file sharing}}.

Packet switching was invented by three groups unaware of each other (Kurose §1.7.1): {{c1::Leonard Kleinrock}} at MIT (1961, 1964), who used {{c1::queueing theory}} to show packet switching suits {{c1::bursty}} traffic; {{c1::Paul Baran}} at RAND (1964), working on {{c1::secure voice for military networks}}; and {{c1::Donald Davies and Roger Scantlebury}} at the {{c1::National Physical Laboratory}} in England.
fields.Extra: Motivation: the telephone network was circuit-switched, which suits constant-rate voice; timeshared computer users generate bursty traffic instead.

fields.Text: Internetworking (Kurose §1.7.2): the architecture for connecting networks together was designed by {{c1::Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn}} in {{c1::1974}}, and the term they coined was {{c1::internetting}}. Early TCP also performed the {{c1::forwarding}} functions now done by IP; the need for an unreliable, non-flow-controlled service for applications such as {{c1::packetised voice}} led to {{c1::IP being split out of TCP}} and to {{c1::UDP}}. TCP, UDP and IP were conceptually in place by {{c1::the end of the 1970s}}.
fields.Extra: This split is what makes the layering of §1.5 possible - and it was driven by an application requirement, not by theory.

fields.Text: Proliferation, 1980-1990 (Kurose §1.7.3): hosts grew from about {{c1::200}} on the ARPAnet at the end of the 1970s to about {{c1::100,000}} by the end of the 1980s. {{c1::NSFNET}} was created in {{c1::1986}} with a backbone starting at {{c1::56 kbps}} and reaching {{c1::1.5 Mbps}} by the end of the decade. TCP/IP replaced NCP on {{c1::January 1, 1983}}, a {{c1::flag day}} on which every host had to switch at once. {{c1::DNS}} and TCP {{c1::congestion control}} (Jacobson, 1988) also date from this decade.
fields.Extra: Other university networks of the period: BITNET (e-mail and file transfer in the US Northeast) and CSNET (for researchers with no ARPAnet access). Nothing like a flag day could be attempted today, which is why IPv6 deployment has taken decades.
